question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician for a 3-week history of intermittent episodes of dizziness. The episodes last for hours at a time and are characterized by the sensation that the room is spinning. The patient also reports that she has started using her cell phone with her left ear because she hears better on that side. She has experienced intermittent ringing and fullness in her right ear. She has no history of serious medical conditions. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F) pulse is 76/min respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. There is horizontal nystagmus to the right. Motor strength is 5/5 in all extremities, and sensory examination shows no abnormalities. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal bilaterally. Weber test shows lateralization to the left ear. The Rinne test is positive bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.opb: Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery
options.ope: Obstruction of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery

analysis: The patient's symptoms of intermittent dizziness, sensation of spinning (vertigo), and hearing issues (ringing and fullness in the right ear) suggest a vestibular disorder. The presence of horizontal nystagmus to the right and the Weber test showing lateralization to the left ear indicates a right-sided issue. The combination of these findings is consistent with a cerebellopontine angle tumor, such as an acoustic neuroma, which can affect the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) and lead to vertigo and hearing loss. Other options do not align as closely with the clinical presentation.
